completed: M2 byte store landed. AllocationRecord.initialized (a list of offsets kept beside the values) is gone; RangeInitialized is read off ByteStore, so it cannot drift from what the writes said.

A run carries initializes as well as bytes, which is required rather than decoration. AccessDescriptor.producesInitialized lets a completed write decline to initialize, and a value-only store would have reported exactly those bytes as initialized because it held values for them -- the permissive direction FOUNDATION.md law 8 forbids. not_initializedAt_write_false is the theorem. Newest wins for initialization as for value, so a non-initializing write over initialized bytes leaves them uninitialized; MEMORY_MODEL.md does not settle that case and this is the reading that cannot admit a program a stricter model would refuse.

Grass/Memory/Apply.lean factors applyAccess out of Op.performAccess: total, executable, with the laws as equations over one function rather than claims about a transition's branches. denialOf moved down with it, since it only ever read a MemoryState.

The section 4 laws that are now proved: applyAccess_refused_preserves_state (the first required law); applyAccess_frames_other_allocation and applyAccess_frames_disjoint_range (framing); applyAccess_comm (reads and writes to disjoint ranges commute).

Commutation is stated as MemoryState.AgreesOn, agreement at every offset, not state equality. That is forced rather than chosen: a journal records two writes in whichever order they arrived, so the orders leave different runs and no proof could make those states equal. Everything downstream reads memory through byteAt?, which is what agrees -- the same reason every ByteStore lemma is over cellAt? rather than runs.

Commutation needed a second half that was easy to miss and is worth flagging to a reviewer. Bytes agreeing is not enough if the decision can move: if a write elsewhere could change whether an access is refused, one order would refuse what the other committed. denialOf_write_of_disjoint and denialOf_write_of_other_allocation rule that out. The initialization clause is the only part of denialOf that reads bytes rather than metadata, and it needed ByteStore.initialized_write_iff_of_disjoint as an iff, not the forward direction alone -- framing must carry a lack of initialization across a write as well as its presence, or an uninitializedRead could be laundered by writing somewhere else.

Op.Oracle.ofMemory replaces Oracle.zeroed. It takes what a store writes and what an indeterminate read observes as parameters, neither defaulted. The second matters: uninitialized bytes have no value to read off the store, denialOf refuses an access demanding allBytesInitialized before the oracle is consulted, so the oracle is reached only where a profile already admitted an indeterminate read and the profile then owes what it observes. Defaulting it to zero would be law 8's permissive fallback wearing a plausible number.

The whole M1 seam fixture runs over the reading oracle unchanged, which is the evidence the store cost no redesign. Four fixtures read values off the recorded trace: a_load_observes_the_prior_store, a_load_before_the_store_observes_the_initial_bytes (the control, without which 0xAB could have been what a load always observes), a_store_leaves_neighbouring_bytes_alone, a_store_leaves_other_allocations_alone. All stated existentially so non-vacuity is part of the claim.
Grass/Memory/Addressing.lean pays the offset-to-address bridge debt Range.lean records: disjoint_ranges_do_not_alias, conditioned on FitsAllocation.

Two duplications removed rather than left: denialOf existed in both Step.lean and Apply.lean, and Oracle.ofMemory rebuilt observedBytes by hand. Same defect as the initialized list -- two copies of a rule can drift, and the one a reader consults need not be the one the transition runs.

completed: M2 section 4's exit criterion is met. runBlock runs a list of accesses in order; byteAt?_write_survives_block discharges a straight-line block, resting on cellAt?_runBlock_of_untouched. The hypothesis is each step's declared range rather than the bytes it actually wrote, which is the weaker fact and the useful one: a caller knows ranges from descriptors and does not know how much data each store carried, and applyAccess only ever writes inside the declared range.

Tests/Memory/StraightLineBlock.lean checks the discharge symbolically rather than concretely, and that choice is the point. A fixture that fixed the allocation, the data and the offsets and closed everything by decide would prove the arithmetic, say nothing about the lemma set, and still compile if every framing theorem were deleted. There the state is universally quantified, the data arbitrary, and every proof one application of a named exported theorem; one local declaration exists and its docstring says it is a wrapper rather than content.

Tests/Memory/Spike1Block.lean runs that discharge on the real instruction mix from Tests/Memory/Spike1Reference.lean: mov transferred 0, the two accesses inside call [rip + __imp_WriteFile], then mov eax transferred. Side conditions are decided because they are what a front end computes; the framing is one application of the theorem, not a decide. The control is there: the same reload IS refused as an uninitializedRead against the state before the store, so the positive result is evidence the initialization check ran rather than evidence it was skipped.

Grass/Memory/Shape.lean discharges STDLIB.md's padding obligation. padding_uninitialized_after_writing_fields is proved for any list of the aggregate's fields in any order with any data, not one schedule. It matters concretely: without it, writing every field of a struct would make the struct read as fully initialized when part of it was never written, and a typed shape could launder an uninitializedRead that denialOf catches on raw bytes. The converse half is proved too, so the two partition the aggregate rather than making a one-sided claim.

The Shape module is deliberately half the row the plan sketched. StructLayout is a Std.Owned facility per STDLIB.md -- it chooses field order, widths, alignment and padding policy and carries an ABI profile -- and none of that is the memory layer's. A Footprint is field ranges and an extent, and its extent is a field rather than derived, because ASSEMBLY_CONSTRUCTION.md section 3 has aggregateAligned, so trailing padding is real and deriving the extent would erase what the module exists to reason about.

Tests/Memory/Padding.lean runs it on a struct that pads for a real reason: a one-byte field, then a four-byte field its alignment puts at offset four. Padding there holds no byte at all rather than an uninitialized one, so a store that quietly zero-filled the gap would fail even with its initialization flags right. general_theorem_applies ties the fixture to the general theorem so a broken proof could not hide behind a fixture that still passed.

applyAccess_state_indep and runBlock_state_indep: what memory looks like afterwards does not depend on what an indeterminate read would have observed. The answer stays in the observation and never reaches memory, so a profile choosing differently changes what a program sees and never what it leaves behind.

Checked against three cases rather than assumed: the original wording is flagged, the fixed wording is not, and the obligation-kind descriptions are not. M2: executable single-thread memory semantics, plus a fix for a soundness defect this branch found in code that had already merged.

Read the defect first. runStep's faulting branch ran the surviving accesses and then performed the faulting substep's access unconditionally, without checking whether the survivors had stopped on a denial. An operation whose first substep was refused still committed its second -- the continue-after-denial behaviour runAccesses exists to prevent, surviving on the one branch runAccesses_stops_at_refusal does not reach. FOUNDATION.md law 8 is the rule it broke. It falsified the closure property section 3.11 of the plan declared closed at M1 freeze, and it is on main now. runStep_stops_at_refusal and runStep_records_no_fault_after_refusal are the theorems; denial_stops_the_operation_on_the_fault_path is the regression, and it checks the store's bytes rather than only the event count, because counting events would not have noticed a write that recorded no event. It was found by local adversarial review with a machine-checked counterexample, not by me.

The M2 work itself. Grass/Memory/ByteStore.lean replaces the per-byte FiniteMap that made a 4KB frame write quadratic; its representation is private, so the exported surface is compaction-stable. A run carries initializes because AccessDescriptor.producesInitialized lets a completed write decline to initialize, and a value-only store would have reported those bytes as initialized -- the permissive direction law 8 forbids. AllocationRecord.initialized is gone; initialization is read off the store. Grass/Memory/Apply.lean is applyAccess with the section 4 laws as equations: refusal preserves state, framing on both axes, and commutation. MemoryState.commit is the single path by which an access commits, so those laws are laws about the transition; performAccess_frames_untouched and runAccesses_frames_untouched state that directly. Grass/Memory/Shape.lean discharges STDLIB.md's padding obligation: padding_uninitialized_after_writing_fields, proved for any list of an aggregate's fields in any order with any data. Grass/Memory/Addressing.lean proves the offset-to-address bridge arithmetic and is NOT wired -- AllocationRecord has no base address -- which section 4.2 records as owed rather than claiming discharged.

What I want adversarial attention on. Section 4.2 lists seven debts, five of which two review rounds found stated as done before I corrected them, so the prose in this branch has a demonstrated tendency to run ahead of the mechanism. In particular: there is no step-level framing theorem and I say so; ByteStore's derived DecidableEq observes the journal and I say so; applyAccess_comm concludes about the state and within one allocation only.
